report:
**Conclusion: the claim is supported, not false.** The strongest direct evidence is a randomized trial in cesarean patients finding that chlorhexidine–alcohol produced a significantly lower 30-day surgical-site-infection (SSI) risk than iodine–alcohol. The primary outcome used CDC SSI definitions. [https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1511048)

The conclusion is also consistent with a cesarean-specific systematic review/meta-analysis of randomized trials, which found lower SSI with chlorhexidine–alcohol than povidone-iodine preparations. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30184558/)

There is reasonable grounds for *qualified* skepticism, but not for reversing the conclusion:

* Not every trial agrees. CAPICA, a single-center pragmatic RCT, reported no less frequent SSI with chlorhexidine–alcohol—but it compared it with **aqueous** povidone-iodine scrub-and-paint, not iodine–alcohol, so it does not directly refute the stated comparison. [https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(17)30723-8/abstract](https://www.ajog.org/article/S0002-9378(17)30723-8/abstract)
* Comparisons can conflate the active antiseptic with formulation, concentration, application technique, and drying time. Thus the evidence supports chlorhexidine–alcohol over iodine–alcohol in the studied cesarean settings, rather than proving universal superiority in every preparation or population.
* An updated RCT meta-analysis still found a benefit in cesarean delivery (eight RCTs; RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.54–0.89), strengthening rather than undermining the claim. [https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1641815/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/medicine/articles/10.3389/fmed.2025.1641815/full)
